clue.text: Look into censure of ski event

indicators.note: into tells us the word for look goes inside the word for censure

parts.note: to slam something is to criticise or censure it harshly
lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: Someone investigates the criticism heaped on a skiing competition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look into' reads like the phrase for investigate, but the two words do separate jobs: 'Look' supplies letters and 'into' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A slalom is a downhill skiing race weaving between gates.

clue.text: Old Catholic heartens the Spanish poet

indicators.note: heartens is read as putting something at the heart of the Spanish article

parts.note: la is the feminine form of the in Spanish
RC stands for Roman Catholic

explanation.surface: An elderly churchman encourages a Spanish versifier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartens' puts O and RC into the middle of LA. Federico García Lorca was a Spanish poet and dramatist.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorca was a celebrated twentieth-century poet from Andalusia.

clue.text: This could make even stalwarts crack up

definitions.text: This could make even stalwarts crack up

indicators.note: crack up suggests the letters of stalwarts break apart and re-form

explanation.surface: One final burden may break down even the toughest supporters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crack up' rearranges STALWARTS. The whole clue also describes the final burden that breaks someone's patience.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverbial final straw is the small extra burden that makes a person finally give way.

clue.text: Complaint caused by knocking back a double spirit

indicators.note: knocking back reads the doubled drink backwards, while hinting at gulping it down
double means the spirit is written twice

parts.note: rum is a spirit

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles after downing a large measure of liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'double' makes RUMRUM and 'knocking back' reverses it. A murmur can be a heart complaint, as well as a quiet grumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A heart murmur is a medical condition, and a murmur is also a muttered grievance.

clue.text: Batters down a barrier in Kent

parts.note: to ram is to batter down with force
a gate is a barrier across an opening

explanation.surface: Someone smashes through a fence somewhere in the Kent countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition 'in Kent' points to a place in the county: Kent is a county in south-east England, and RAMSGATE is a seaside town there.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramsgate is a port town on the Kent coast, so it is a place found in that county.

clue.text: As immobile as a well-established tree

explanation.surface: A tree long grown in place cannot move at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone frozen with fear stays fixed in place, and a tree with deep roots literally stands fixed in its location.

clue.text: Mark, his ham's awful — a real mess

indicators.note: awful suggests these letters are in a terrible jumble

parts.note: taken as written
the possessive ending is kept as an S here

explanation.surface: Someone tells Mark his overacting is dreadful and chaotic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' rearranges M, HIS and HAMS. 'ham' here is an overacting performer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mishmash is a confused jumble or hotchpotch.

clue.text: Admit it's good to let off steam

parts.note: to rant is to vent anger noisily

explanation.surface: Someone concedes that venting anger is healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: To grant a point is to concede or acknowledge it.

clue.text: So the sappers get a warning of course

parts.note: taken as written
RE is the Royal Engineers, whose soldiers are called sappers
fore is the golfer's shout warning of a ball heading towards others on the course

explanation.surface: Army engineers are naturally told about danger beforehand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally' but means on a golf course, where FORE is shouted.
explanation.definitionFit: Therefore means consequently or for that reason, a meaning shared by this conjunction.

clue.text: Informer has origins in the rank and file

parts.note: a grass is British slang for a police informer
roots are origins or sources

explanation.surface: A police informant comes from humble working-class beginnings.
explanation.walkthrough: GRASS is British slang for someone who informs to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: The grass roots of a movement are its ordinary members, the people below the leadership.

clue.text: Race around a tree

indicators.note: around suggests the letters of race are moved about into a new order

explanation.surface: Runners sprint in a loop round a single tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' rearranges RACE to make ACER.
explanation.definitionFit: Acer is the botanical genus of maples, a kind of tree.

clue.text: Rubber carried by a ship in French river

indicators.note: in tells us the letters for a ship go inside the name of the river

parts.note: the Meuse is a river flowing through France
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: An eraser is transported by boat along a river in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubber' looks like an eraser or tyre material but means a person who rubs; 'in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A masseuse is a woman who gives massages, someone who rubs clients' muscles.

clue.text: Joints go to bishops' heads

explanation.surface: Carpentry joints somehow end up on top of senior clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition describes the tall pointed hats worn by bishops, the things that go on bishops' heads.
explanation.definitionFit: A mitre is a woodwork joint cut at an angle, and also a bishop's tall ceremonial headdress.

clue.text: Fish served in a rich, aromatic sauce

indicators.note: served in signals that the fish is found inside the words rich aromatic

explanation.surface: A fish is presented in a spicy, fragrant sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served in' finds CHAR running across 'riCH ARomatic'.
explanation.definitionFit: Char is a freshwater fish related to the trout.

clue.text: A simple manufacturer

parts.note: a simple is an old word for a medicinal plant, so someone who prepares such remedies makes simples

explanation.surface: A plain, unsophisticated maker of goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'simple' looks like an adjective describing the maker, but is a noun: a herb used as a remedy.
explanation.definitionFit: A herbalist prepares remedies from medicinal plants, once called simples.

clue.text: He leaves a tin-opener and broken-down toaster

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter, so take the start of tin
broken-down suggests the letters of toaster are smashed apart and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone bequeaths a tin-opener and a toaster that no longer works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opener' gives T, the first letter of 'tin', and 'broken-down' rearranges TOASTER as ESTATOR. 'He leaves' means a man who leaves property in a will, not one departing.
explanation.definitionFit: A testator is a person who makes a will, bequeathing possessions to heirs.

clue.text: Material from which altar base is made

indicators.note: is made suggests the letters of altar base are fashioned into something new

explanation.surface: This describes the stone used to build a church altar's base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is made' rearranges ALTAR BASE. The surface works literally too, as altars are often made of this stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Alabaster is a soft white stone used for carving.

clue.text: Heather keeps promise, despite abhorrence

indicators.note: keeps means the plant word holds the word for promise inside it

parts.note: ling is another name for common heather
an oath is a solemn promise

explanation.surface: A woman named Heather honours her vow despite deep hatred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heather' looks like a woman's name but is the plant; 'keeps' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Loathing is intense hatred or disgust.

clue.text: Induced to talk — but rather stretched

explanation.surface: A reluctant witness was coaxed into speaking, though it took ages.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw someone out is to coax them into speaking, and something drawn out is prolonged.

clue.text: Article we sent back again

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: sent back means the word we is read backwards

explanation.surface: We returned a piece of writing to start over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' turns WE into EW.
explanation.definitionFit: Anew means once more or afresh.

clue.text: Get in a high-speed car, however horrified

indicators.note: in tells us the word for get goes inside the car abbreviation

parts.note: GT stands for gran turismo, a fast touring car
to have or get, as in he has a cold

explanation.surface: Someone climbs into a sports car, though terrified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get in' reads as climbing into the car, but 'Get' supplies letters (has, as in 'has a cold') and 'in' signals the container; 'however' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Aghast means struck with horror or shock.

clue.text: Ill fortune is maybe what he deserves

definitions.text: Ill fortune is maybe what he deserves

parts.words: Ill fortune is maybe what he deserves
parts.note: a rogue's misfortune is a bad share of fate, and the rogue himself is called by the same two-word phrase

explanation.surface: Someone thinks a scoundrel has earned his misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'lot' is one's fortune or fate, so a bad one is ill fortune; the same phrase is also a name for a rascal, the 'he' who deserves it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bad lot is a dishonest person, and a bad lot in life is misfortune.

clue.text: Proposition found in many Jane Austen novel

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, so it can mean many
Emma is a novel by Jane Austen

explanation.surface: A theory is discovered within a classic English novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'many' gives L, the Roman fifty, a crossword convention for a large number.
explanation.definitionFit: A lemma is a subsidiary proposition proved in order to establish a theorem.

clue.text: Inscribed round a tomb finally

indicators.note: round signals that the word for finally wraps around the tomb

parts.note: in the end, finally; end stands for finally
a grave is a tomb

explanation.surface: Words were carved around a burial place in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' is the container signal; 'finally' stands for its synonym 'in the end', giving the outer word.
explanation.definitionFit: Engraved means carved or inscribed into a surface such as stone.

clue.text: Gong sounded by one's host

indicators.note: sounded signals the abbreviation is spoken as letters

parts.note: a gong is slang for a medal, and MC is the Military Cross

explanation.surface: A host strikes a gong to call guests.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, MC gives EMCEE. A 'gong' is British slang for a medal, here the Military Cross.
explanation.definitionFit: An emcee is a master of ceremonies, someone who hosts an event.

clue.text: Determined to be in business

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to work in commerce.
explanation.definitionFit: Firm means resolute or unwavering, and a firm is a company.

clue.text: Actually employed as a solicitor

explanation.surface: Someone really is working as a lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: A solicitor is a British lawyer who handles legal work outside the higher courts; such lawyers are said to be in practice.
explanation.definitionFit: In practice means in reality, and a lawyer working professionally is said to be in practice.

clue.text: Honestly, it isn't crooked

explanation.surface: Someone vouches truthfully that a thing is not bent.
explanation.definitionFit: Straight can mean frankly or honestly, and a straight line has no bends.

clue.text: Jack needs to become objective

parts.note: a jack tar, or tar, is a sailor
to get can mean to become, as in get angry

explanation.surface: A man named Jack must turn impartial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a name, but crosswords use it for a sailor, TAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A target is a goal or aim one strives for.
